messages.subject: adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
parts:
[now on stan-dev]

(Peter this would be something good for you to do if you're
looking for something light and distracting until I get the
traits fixed for distributions.)

More below.

On 5/7/13 2:05 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>...
> It might be slightly faster if you would use the square() and sqrt() functions instead of the the pow(x,k) function that
> takes an arbitrary exponent. But I doubt that is slowing you down a noticeable amount.

Not much gain. We have the following in the code.

inline var pow(const var& base, const double exponent) {
if (exponent == 0.5)
return sqrt(base);
if (exponent == 1.0)
return base;
if (exponent == 2.0)
return base * base; // FIXME: square() functionality from special_functions
return var(new pow_vd_vari(base.vi_,exponent));
}

Now that we have square(), the base * base should be replaced.

Should I include the negative ones, too? This is one reason I've
been meaning to add special functions:

// precision->variance, variance->precision
inv(x) = 1/x.

// deviation->precision
inv_square(x) = 1 / x^2

// precision->deviation
inv_sqrt(x) = 1 / sqrt(x)

These seem to get used a lot in transforms, so they'd absolutely
be worth doing in both basic and vectorized forms (though as Ben
says, the vectorization here would be for convenience, not speed, unless
we want to use some of the nifty tricks Marcus developed for matrices
to reduce virtual function calls).

- Bob

To do this would either require moving to either (a) expression
templates so we can do it on the C++ side, or (b) code analysis
in the generator. Either would let us evaluate 1/sqrt(x) with
an efficient inv_sqrt() that efficiently calculates derivatives,
which is the whole point. It's not for more expressiveness.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
parts:
On 5/7/13 4:46 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> I'm not sure I was totally clear. I was just proposing that we allow
> elementwise division to broadcast scalars to vectors.
We already support that.

> It wouldn't have
> a significant effect on speed, it'd just be cleaner.
>
> Is there any speed benefit to specializing 1/x using an inv() function?

Yes, at least in the current implementation. Division of double
by var uses this implementation:

class divide_dv_vari : public op_dv_vari {
public:
divide_dv_vari(double a, vari* bvi) :
op_dv_vari(a / bvi->val_, a, bvi) {
}
void chain() {
bvi_->adj_ -= adj_ * ad_ / (bvi_->val_ * bvi_->val_);
}
};


So there's an extra 8 bytes stored for the double, extra
sets in the constructor, division by a non-static variable
and multiplication. With inv(), it's simpler:

class inv_vari : public op_v_vari {
public:
inv_vari(vari* bvi) :
op_dv_vari(1 / bvi->val_, bvi) {
}
void chain() {
bvi_->adj_ -= adj_ / (bvi_->val_ * bvi_->val_);
}
};

I doubt it's a huge deal, which is why I haven't done it yet.
The argument's even stronger for inv_sqrt or inv_square, though,
which involve an extra virtual function call and a whole new
vari on the stack for the sqrt().

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
parts:
On 5/23/13 4:51 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> Do we still need to implement the special functions inv(x), inv_square(x), inv_sqrt(x)? If so, I'll get on this. Are
> there any other special functions we want to implement?

Yes, that'd be great. Then add them as special cases
to the pow() implementations, which is where they'll
probably get used the most.

There are many functions we'd like to have listed in
the to-do. But I'd recommend cleaning up some of what you
have done for fvar already before doing any new functions.
Make sure there are no repeated expensive sub-operations,
like exp() or log(). And fix up the matrix ops like
mdivide_left to do the derivatives explicitly. The way
it is now, using a direct auto-dif on inverse will be both
slow and have bad numerical properties. Try to follow
the way it's done for reverse-mode and look at the Giles
paper I sent.

There's also log_minus_exp(). You should take a look
at the attached paper. One thing you could do is look
more seriously at our arithmetic accuracy in functions
like this and log_sum_exp and related functions. There's
a ref to get started next to the log_minus_exp() discussion
on the to-do list.

A much trickier request we got was for Chebyshev
polynomials. I don't really even understand what the
original poster was asking for, but if you can
figure that out and implement it using Boost, that'd
be nice. Especially if you could come up with an application
example.

Even a crude Kronecker product (just the brute force
multiply) would be good to have.

A function to_vector() that applies to matrices and
dumps them out in column-major order would be nice.

It would also be good to expose the special functions that
were added as helpers in doing the cumulative distributions.

Some other harder operations include things like a quadratic
form for matrices, also listed in the to-do list.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
parts:
On 5/23/13 6:04 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> What if we don't know if x is auto-diff or double, as is the case with most of the fvar functions since x could be an
> fvar or rev?

I'd go with (x * x) in that case.

To squeeze more efficiency out, you can always specialize.
So instead of having fvar<T>, you'd have
fvar<fvar<T>> or fvar<var>, which could use pow() because
you know they'll be called with either an fvar or a var.
The plain old T case can then do it with (x * x).

What we do in the probability functions is use trait templates
like so:

if (is_arithmetic<T>::value)
y = x * x;
else
y = pow(x,2);

where is_arithmetic is a Boost type traits class.

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/type_traits/doc/html/boost_typetraits/reference/is_arithmetic.html

The compiler will evaluate the boolean at compile time and
should be able to eliminate the unneeded branch and avoid
any branch prediction or evaluation at run time.

Whether this is worth it or not depends on the cost savings
and how many times it gets called. If neither are expected
to be high, I'd go with something simpler. The downside for
something more complex like the above is that it is harder to
read for others looking at the code later.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
parts:
On 6/12/13 10:46 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> For to_vector(), what's the return type? vector of vectors?

Just a vector. The point is to convert a matrix
to a vector. As in:

matrix[M,N] a;
vector[M * N] b;

b <- to_vector(a);

And it should probably be dumped out column major for
efficiency:

a[m,n] == b[(n - 1) * M + m]

e.g., for M = 2, N = 3

b[1] = a[1,1]
b[2] = a[2,1]
b[3] = a[1,2]
b[4] = a[2,2]
b[5] = a[1,3]
b[6] = a[2,3]

This should be able to be done without iterating by
grabbing the data of an Eigen matrix, which is an
array in column-major order. You can then probably
use Eigen::Map to construct the vector to return.

The reason this is nice is that we can use it to vectorize
some operations like univariate densities to matrices without making
the user write out a loop.

This shouldn't be much work, but it's also not a super high
priority.

- Bob
